title: Global Inequality & Development
hook: Where you're born still shapes your life chances more than almost anything else. Closing that gap between rich and poor nations is one of politics' great unfinished projects.
key_points: Vast gaps in wealth and well-being persist between and within countries.
'Development' means improving living standards — incomes, health, education, opportunity.
Debated drivers include history, institutions, geography, trade, and governance.
Tools include aid, trade access, debt relief, and investment — none a sole cure.
content_html: One of the starkest facts about the modern world is how much a person's life prospects — their income, health, schooling, and life expectancy — depend on the accident of where they were born. Enormous gaps in wealth and well-being separate rich and poor countries, and large gaps persist within countries too. "Development" is the term for the project of closing those gaps: raising living standards so that more people have decent incomes, health care, education, and opportunity. It has been a central concern of global politics since the mid-20th century, when many newly independent nations sought to catch up with wealthier ones.
extra_html: Why some countries grew rich while others stayed poor is one of the most debated questions in the field, and the World Bank and similar institutions track the patterns closely. Proposed explanations include the legacies of history such as colonialism, the quality of a country's institutions and governance (whether they protect property, curb corruption, and provide public goods), geography and natural resources, and access to trade and investment. Most analysts now emphasize that no single factor explains everything and that institutions and governance matter a great deal. The same humility applies to the tools used to promote development: foreign aid, access to rich-country markets, debt relief, foreign investment, and good domestic policy can each help, but decades of experience show that none is a magic cure on its own. Global inequality endures partly because its causes are tangled and partly because addressing it requires sustained cooperation and reform — making it as much a political challenge as an economic one.

related.title: Globalization
related.hook: The world's economies have woven together so tightly that a decision in one country ripples through all the others — that deepening interdependence is globalization.

related.title: Trade & Protectionism
related.hook: Should a country trade freely with the world or shield its own industries? This single question has driven economic politics for centuries — and still does.

related.title: The Welfare State
related.hook: Should the state guarantee a floor below which no one can fall? The welfare state is modern government's answer — and one of its biggest, most-debated commitments.

flashcards.prompt: What does 'development' mean in global political economy?
flashcards.back_html: Improving living standards — incomes, health, education, and opportunity — especially in poorer countries.

flashcards.prompt: Which is offered as a driver of differences in national development?

choices.text: Institutions, history, geography, trade, and quality of governance
Only the climate, and nothing else
Purely random chance with no causes

flashcards.explanation_html: Scholars debate a mix of factors — especially institutions and governance, alongside history, geography, and trade.

flashcards.prompt: What is true of tools like aid, trade access, and debt relief?

choices.text: Each can help, but none is a sole cure for underdevelopment
Aid alone reliably ends poverty everywhere

flashcards.explanation_html: Development tools can each contribute, but no single instrument resolves a problem with many interacting causes.
